title: The Carpet Merchant Who Decoded Cuneiform
event_summary: In 1857, the Royal Asiatic Society conducted a remarkable blind test: four scholars were each given sealed copies of a newly discovered Assyrian inscription and asked to translate it independently. Among them was Henry Rawlinson, a British officer, but the translation that stunned the committee came from Edward Hincks, an impoverished Irish rector who had been systematically deciphering cuneiform from his parish with almost no funding. When all four translations substantially agreed, the Society declared cuneiform officially deciphered — unlocking thousands of years of Mesopotamian history, law, literature, and science that had been completely lost to humanity.
why_forgotten: Rawlinson, the military adventurer who had physically copied inscriptions from the cliff face at Behistun, became the celebrated hero of cuneiform studies, while Hincks — who arguably made the deeper intellectual breakthroughs in understanding the syllabic nature of the script — died in poverty and obscurity. Victorian Britain preferred stories of imperial daring over scholarly parish work, and Hincks's Irish origins during the post-Famine era further marginalized his contributions.
why_it_matters: The decipherment of cuneiform revealed the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Code of Hammurabi, and flood narratives that fundamentally challenged Biblical literalism, reshaping theology, comparative religion, and the entire field of ancient history. It proved that complex legal systems, literature, and mathematics existed millennia before Greece and Rome, demolishing the Eurocentric origin story of civilization. Every modern understanding of the ancient Near East — from Abraham's Ur to the origins of writing itself — flows directly from this moment.
